title: I built a desktop app that lets Claude trade your Robinhood account. Paper mode is free, looking for people to break it.
author: BFitch85
selftext:
Some context before the pitch, because I think it matters for whether this is useful to you.

It runs on your machine, not our servers. Your Robinhood login and your Anthropic API key are encrypted by your OS and never sent to us. We never touch your funds. The tradeoff is real and cuts the other way too: if your computer is off, the agent is not running.

You write the strategy in plain English. It drives a fixed set of about 22 tools (quotes, historicals, option chains, technical indicators, a volume metric) and proposes one trade per cycle (you set up tasks with the strategy, account, and run frequency in minutes). Risk limits are enforced in code, not in the prompt, so a strategy cannot talk its way past your position caps or daily trade limit.

Paper mode is free and always will be. Simulated fills against live quotes, in a separate paper account. Same strategies, same guardrails, same approval flow. You need a Robinhood connection for live prices and your own Anthropic API key for the reasoning, so it is not zero setup, and it is not zero cost per cycle. I would rather say that now than have you find out after installing. (strategy and tool definitions are re-read from cache every cycle to cut costs)

What I actually want: people who will run it for a couple of weeks in paper and tell me where it is wrong. (or with your live agentic account. my wife and I run ours regularly, the harness works, it's the strategy that affects good and bad days. I have been calibrating the volume signal this month and found that my own metric was structurally biased low, which made a "40% above normal" threshold really a 90th percentile filter. That is the kind of thing I only found by staring at real sessions. There is more of it in there.

If you run paper for a bit and come back with something concrete, I will give you a two week live key, no card. That is a real offer but it is second, not first, because handing out live trading access to a brand new bot seems like a bad idea for both of us.

Honest limitations: Windows only right now. Robinhood is the fully supported broker, Public works for a narrower set of tools. It is new, I have almost no users, and I cannot tell you it makes money. There is a back-tester in the app for classical strategies (moving average crossover, RSI, opening range breakout, VWAP reversion) against real Robinhood history. What it cannot do yet is replay the AI agent itself, so it can show you how a rule-based strategy would have done, but it cannot yet show you how the Claude-driven one would have done. That is the next thing I am building.

Happy to answer anything, including the uncomfortable questions.

comments.author: Interesting_Gold_792
comments.body:
The separation between the agent and deterministic risk controls is the part I like most here. Letting the model propose a trade while code retains veto authority seems much safer than putting risk constraints in the prompt.  
Your point about the volume metric being structurally biased is interesting too. That’s exactly the kind of issue that can look perfectly reasonable until enough real sessions expose it.  
I’m especially curious about the AI-agent replay you’re building next. How are you planning to make historical replay deterministic enough to evaluate? Are you going to persist the exact market snapshot/tool responses the agent saw at each decision point and replay those, rather than letting the model query reconstructed historical data?  
And when evaluating the agent, are you planning to compare only PnL, or also decision stability, rejected/vetoed trades, expectancy and drawdown? I’d be really interested in how you’re approaching that layer.

replies.author: BFitch85
replies.body:
Yeah, I noticed it more after some volume measurement changes. Some large-cap 5 minute bars were coming back at a fraction of their neighbours' volume, which is why the baseline is a median now. Reconstructed data smooths that out, so replaying the recorded responses is the plan rather than rebuilding the snapshot. Right now I log the calls and the reasoning per run but not the full responses, so that part needs widening first.

Still all down to the strategy you write. Those are parameters that are available, none of them fire on their own.

On evaluating it, I had the agent reasoning over its own recent trades early on and that skewed it. It started shying away from entries to protect a rough stretch. It doesn't see its day P&L now for that reason.

Not sure P/L should be the only measure either, win rate maybe. I hadn't thought about scoring the rejected and vetoed trades, that's a good call. Though I can already see the code veto firing on about 1 in 9 of what the model proposes, so there's clearly something in there worth looking at.

And backtests don't guarantee forward results, so I lean on paper mode more. Partly to check nothing's broken, but mostly to see whether I actually like its entries before I turn it loose on autonomous. 

Any suggestions?

replies.author: Interesting_Gold_792
replies.body:
I think the 1-in-9 veto rate is actually one of the most interesting datasets you have.

If I were evaluating this, I’d preserve every proposed trade before the deterministic gate touches it, including the market/tool snapshot, model reasoning, proposed entry/size, which gate accepted or rejected it, and the reason for the veto. Then I’d forward-track the rejected trade hypothetically without ever executing it.

That gives you two populations over time: accepted proposals vs vetoed proposals. Then you can ask whether the gates are actually removing negative expectancy/risk, or accidentally filtering good trades too.

I’d also avoid making win rate the main score. I’d probably look at expectancy, profit factor, avg winner vs avg loser, max drawdown, number of trades, and maybe decision stability when the same/similar snapshot is evaluated more than once.

The P&L observation is really interesting too. The fact that showing recent performance changed future decisions is almost an experiment by itself. I’d keep outcome feedback separate from the market evidence unless the strategy explicitly needs portfolio state.

And I agree with leaning heavily on paper/forward observation. Replay can tell you whether the logic behaves as intended, but forward paper is where timing, data quality and things you didn’t know to model tend to show up.

I’d be very curious what those \~1-in-9 vetoed trades look like after you’ve accumulated enough of them.

comments.author: fomoz
comments.body: Or just let Claude Code trade for you. It's cheaper in inference cost and no need for a third party app that's not free. I really don't see what you're trying to offer there.

replies.author: BFitch85
replies.body:
Fair, and the inference cost point is just true. If you're on a Max plan, Claude Code plus the Robinhood MCP is cheaper than paying per token, and for a hands-on session it is probably better. I'd use it that way myself.

The difference is what happens when you're not at the keyboard. Claude Code runs when you run it. This runs a task every N minutes on its own and has to survive its own bad decisions without you there.

Concretely: your risk limits are code, not prompt. In Claude Code "don't exceed $1000 a trade" is a sentence the model can reason its way around, and it will, because it is trying to be helpful. Here the guardrail runs after the proposal and outside the model's reach. Across my log it has vetoed 178 of 1,531 proposals. A prompt cannot do that to itself.

Same for the things that happen between cycles: a stop attached the moment a fill lands, trailing exits on an 8 second poll, a circuit breaker that halts the day on realized loss, and an order repriced to the live quote at execution instead of at analysis time. None of that is the model's job, and none of it exists if the agent only runs while you're watching it.

So it isn't a cheaper Claude Code. If you want to sit there and direct it, use Claude Code, genuinely. If you want something running at 10:47 while you're in a meeting, with limits it cannot argue past and an audit log of every decision, that's a different product.
